claims.claim: Only three regions, including the bed nucleus of stria terminalis, extended amygdala, and parabrachial nucleus, contained high densities of labeling.
claims.source: Most of the brain regions identified had either few or moderate numbers of terminals, with only three regions, including the bed nucleus of stria terminalis, extended amygdala, and parabrachial nucleus, containing high densities of labeling (Figure 1C–D and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C-D and Table 1.

claims.claim: No terminal labeling was observed in cortical regions of any of the five brains evaluated.
claims.source: Consistent with previous studies using traditional anterograde tracers in the CeA (Aggleton, 2000; Barbier et al., 2017; Reardon and Mitrofanis, 2000; Shinonaga et al., 1992; Zhou et al., 2018), no terminal labeling was observed in cortical regions of any of the five brains evaluated.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Moderate CeA-PKCδ axonal terminal labeling was observed between rostral-caudal levels 1.46 mm and 2.70 mm posterior to bregma in the ZI.
claims.source: As illustrated in the representative images in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, moderate CeA-PKCδ axonal terminal labeling was observed between rostral-caudal levels 1.46 mm and 2.70 mm posterior to bregma.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: CeA-PKCδ terminals were restricted to the middle and ventral sectors of the ZI in all brains analyzed.
claims.source: Mapping of the distribution of CeA-PKCδ terminals within the ZI further showed that these axonal terminals were restricted to the middle and ventral sectors of the ZI in all brains analyzed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: CTB-647 was detected in CeA-PKCδ neurons, validating the anatomical projection from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI.
claims.source: Notably, CTB-647 was detected in CeA-PKCδ neurons (Figure 2B), validating the anatomical projection from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Approximately 19% of CTB-positive CeA neurons are also positive for PKCδ-tdTomato.
claims.source: Quantification of CeA neurons positive for both CTB-647 and PKCδ-tdTomato further revealed that approximately 19% of CTB-positive CeA neurons are also positive for PKCδ-tdTomato.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results based on quantification.

claims.claim: Neurons positive for both CTB-647 and PKCδ-tdTomato were limited to the capsular and lateral subdivisions of the CeA.
claims.source: As illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, neurons positive for both CTB-647 and PKCδ-tdTomato were limited to the capsular and lateral subdivisions of the CeA, with higher densities observed in the middle/posterior regions of the CeA, between rostral-caudal levels 1.34 and 1.70 posterior to bregma.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: CeA-PKCδ neurons in the capsular and lateral CeA send inputs with moderate densities of terminals to the middle and ventral sectors of the ZI.
claims.source: Together, the results from our anatomical experiments show that CeA-PKCδ neurons in the capsular and lateral CeA send inputs with moderate densities of terminals to the middle and ventral sectors of the ZI.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on anatomical data.

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of ChR2-expressing CeA terminals in the ZI showed robust inhibitory post-synaptic currents in 60% of VGAT-positive cells.
claims.source: Optogenetic stimulation of ChR2-expressing CeA terminals in the ZI with blue light further showed robust inhibitory post-synaptic currents in 60% of VGAT-positive cells (12 out of 20 cells; Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Optically evoked postsynaptic responses occurred in the presence of TTX and 4-AP, demonstrating that the inputs from the CeA to the ZI are monosynaptic.
claims.source: Optically evoked postsynaptic responses occurred in the presence of TTX and 4-AP, demonstrating that the inputs from the CeA to the ZI are monosynaptic.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results based on electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: 53% of VGAT-negative ZI neurons display inhibitory post-synaptic currents in response to optical stimulation of ChR2-expressing CeA terminals.
claims.source: Of note, recordings in VGAT-negative ZI neurons revealed that 53% (8 out of 15 cells) of these ZI neurons also display inhibitory post-synaptic currents in response to optical stimulation of ChR2-expressing CeA terminals.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results based on electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Paired pulse ratio is indistinguishable between VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons, demonstrating that CeA-synaptic inputs are comparable in VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons.
claims.source: Quantification of the responses to optical paired stimulation further showed that paired pulse ratio is indistinguishable between VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons, demonstrating that CeA-synaptic inputs are comparable in VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The mean oIPSC amplitude in response to blue light stimulation was reduced after bath exchange to 10 µM bicuculline.
claims.source: As illustrated in the representative traces and graph in Figure 2E, the mean oIPSC amplitude in response to blue light stimulation (470 nm, 10 mW) was reduced after bath exchange to 10 µM bicuculline.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Recordings at a holding potential of –70 mV showed either no response to blue light stimulation or a small inward current in neurons that showed robust light-evoked outward currents at holding potential of 0 mV.
claims.source: Parallel recordings at a holding potential of –70 mV (near reversal potential for chloride) further showed either no response to blue light stimulation or a small inward current in neurons that showed robust light-evoked outward currents at holding potential of 0 mV (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The projection from the CeA to the ZI is inhibitory.
claims.source: Together, these findings confirm that the projection from the CeA to the ZI is inhibitory.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Bath application of CNO significantly inhibited firing responses in hM4Di-transduced neurons.
claims.source: As illustrated in Figure 3A, bath application of the DREADD ligand clozapine N-oxide (CNO; 10 µM) significantly inhibited firing responses in hM4Di-transduced neurons, with no measurable effect observed in response to bath application of the saline vehicle control.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Transduction of hM4Di was restricted to the ZI.
claims.source: Histological verification of injection sites at the end of the experiments further demonstrated that transduction of hM4Di was restricted to the ZI (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The numbers and rostral-caudal distribution of transduced cells within the ZI of mice stereotaxically injected with hM4Di was comparable to the numbers and rostral-caudal distribution of VGAT-positive cells in the ZI of VGAT-cre::Ai9 mice, demonstrating robust transduction efficiency.
claims.source: The numbers and rostral-caudal distribution of transduced cells within the ZI of mice stereotaxically injected with hM4Di was comparable to the numbers and rostral-caudal distribution of VGAT-positive cells in the ZI of VGAT-cre::Ai9 mice, demonstrating robust transduction efficiency (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Following cuff implantation on the sciatic nerve, tactile and pressure sensitivity was significantly lower in the hindpaw ipsilateral to cuff implantation compared to the contralateral hindpaw or either hindpaw in sham treated mice.
claims.source: As expected, following cuff implantation on the sciatic nerve, tactile and pressure sensitivity was significantly lower in the hindpaw ipsilateral to cuff implantation compared to the contralateral hindpaw or either hindpaw in sham treated mice (Figure 3E and F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E and F.

claims.claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons resulted in robust bilateral hypersensitivity to tactile and pressure stimulation in sham mice.
claims.source: As illustrated in Figure 3E and F, chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons resulted in robust bilateral hypersensitivity to tactile and pressure stimulation in sham mice as well as contralateral hypersensitivity in cuff-implanted mice.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E and F.

claims.claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons resulted in contralateral hypersensitivity in cuff-implanted mice.
claims.source: As illustrated in Figure 3E and F, chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons resulted in robust bilateral hypersensitivity to tactile and pressure stimulation in sham mice as well as contralateral hypersensitivity in cuff-implanted mice.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E and F.

claims.claim: Withdrawal thresholds in the hindpaw ipsilateral to cuff treatment were indistinguishable before and after chemogenetic inactivation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons.
claims.source: Withdrawal thresholds in the hindpaw ipsilateral to cuff treatment were indistinguishable before and after chemogenetic inactivation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons, demonstrating that inhibition of ZI cells does not measurably affect cuff-induced hypersensitivity to tactile and pressure stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results.

claims.claim: Inhibition of ZI VGAT-positive neurons is sufficient to elicit hypersensitivity in the absence of injury that resembles the hypersensitivity observed following sciatic nerve cuff implantation.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that inhibition of ZI VGAT-positive neurons is sufficient to elicit hypersensitivity in the absence of injury that resembles the hypersensitivity observed following sciatic nerve cuff implantation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claims.claim: The effects of chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons on tactile and pressure sensitivity were transient.
claims.source: The effects of chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons on tactile and pressure sensitivity were transient, as paw withdrawal thresholds in all treated animals returned to pre-injection values 1 day following CNO injections.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claims.claim: Behavioral responses to cold and heat stimulation of the hindpaws were unaltered by chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI in all animals tested.
claims.source: Behavioral responses to cold and heat stimulation of the hindpaws, however, were unaltered by chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI in all animals tested.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claims.claim: Inhibition of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI is sufficient to induce hypersensitivity in the absence of injury in a modality-specific manner.
claims.source: Taken together, the results from these chemogenetic experiments demonstrate that inhibition of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI is sufficient to induce hypersensitivity in the absence of injury in a modality-specific manner.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claims.claim: i.p. injection of CNO resulted in robust c-Fos expression in the ZI of VGAT-cre animals injected with hM3Dq.
claims.source: As illustrated in Figure 4D and i.p. injection of CNO resulted in robust c-Fos expression in the ZI of VGAT-cre animals injected with hM3Dq, compared to the c-Fos expression observed in the ZI of saline-injected control mice that also expressed hM3Dq or CNO-injected control VGAT-cre mice stereotaxically injected with the control virus.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: c-Fos expression in hM3Dq-transduced cells is significantly higher in CNO-treated mice than in saline-treated mice or in mCherry-transduced neurons from CNO-treated mice.
claims.source: Quantification of ZI cells co-expressing c-Fos and mCherry further confirmed that c-Fos expression in hM3Dq-transduced cells is significantly (p<0.05) higher in CNO-treated mice than in saline-treated mice or in mCherry-transduced neurons from CNO-treated mice (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: CNO-mediated activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons led to significant reversal of cuff-induced hypersensitivity in the hindpaw ipsilateral to cuff implantation.
claims.source: CNO-mediated activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons led to significant (p<0.0001) reversal of cuff-induced hypersensitivity in the hindpaw ipsilateral to cuff implantation, while no measurable effects were seen in saline-injected or CNO-injected mCherry-control mice.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claims.claim: The effects of activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons were specific to nerve injury.
claims.source: The effects of activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons were specific to nerve injury as withdrawal thresholds in sham-treated mice or the hindpaw contralateral to sciatic nerve cuff were comparable between groups.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claims.claim: Reversal of cuff-induced hypersensitivity by activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons was modality-specific.
claims.source: As illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-D, reversal of cuff-induced hypersensitivity was also modality-specific as behavioral responses to cold and heat stimulation of the hindpaws were unaffected by chemogenetic activation of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-D.

claims.claim: Activation of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI reverses cuff-induced pain hypersensitivity in a modality-specific manner.
claims.source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that activation of VGAT-positive neurons in the ZI reverses cuff-induced pain hypersensitivity in a modality-specific manner.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on behavioral data.

claims.claim: Yellow light stimulation significantly inhibited firing responses in NpHR-positive CeA cells but had no measurable effect in neighboring NpHR-negative neurons.
claims.source: Whole-cell current-clamp recordings of neurons expressing NpHR-mCherry in acute CeA slices confirmed that yellow light (590 nm, 10 mW) stimulation significantly (p<0.0001) inhibited firing responses in NpHR-positive CeA cells but had no measurable effect in neighboring NpHR-negative neurons (Figure 5E), further validating our experimental approach.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in the ZI with yellow light significantly reduced cuff-induced hypersensitivity to pinch stimulation of the treated paw without affecting the untreated paw.
claims.source: At the behavioral level, optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in the ZI with yellow light (561 nm, 10 mW) significantly (p<0.0001) reduced cuff-induced hypersensitivity to pinch stimulation of the treated paw without affecting the untreated paw (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Yellow light-mediated behavioral effects were dependent on laser intensity.
claims.source: Yellow light-mediated behavioral effects were dependent on laser intensity, with increasing laser intensities resulting in larger reductions of cuff-induced hypersensitivity at intensities between 0.04 and 0.06 mW, and with a plateau observed at intensities equal to or higher than 0.07 mW (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI resulted in significant reductions of cuff-induced hypersensitivity to tactile, cold, and heat stimulation of the treated hindpaw at both 0.07 mW and 10 mW laser intensities.
claims.source: As illustrated in Figure 6A–D, optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI resulted in significant (p<0.0001) reductions of cuff-induced hypersensitivity to tactile (Figure 6B), cold (Figure 6C), and heat (Figure 6D) stimulation of the treated hindpaw at both 0.07 mW and 10 mW laser intensities.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A-D.

claims.claim: Injury-induced activation of the CeA-PKCδ to ZI inhibitory pathway is necessary for cuff-induced pressure, tactile, and thermal hypersensitivity.
claims.source: Altogether, these results indicate that injury-induced activation of the CeA-PKCδ to ZI inhibitory pathway is necessary for cuff-induced pressure, tactile, and thermal hypersensitivity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on optogenetic behavioral data.

claims.claim: Activation of CeA-PKCδ neurons induces bilateral tactile hypersensitivity in the absence of injury.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that activation of CeA-PKCδ neurons induces bilateral tactile hypersensitivity in the absence of injury Wilson et al., 2019.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Blue light stimulation significantly increased firing responses in ChR2-positive CeA cells but had no measurable effect in control ChR2-negative neighboring neurons.
claims.source: Whole-cell current-clamp recordings of neurons expressing ChR2-mCherry in acute CeA slices further confirmed that blue light (470 nm, 10 mW) stimulation significantly (P<0.0001) increased firing responses in ChR2-positive CeA cells but had no measurable effect in control ChR2-negative neighboring neurons (Figure 7E–G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7E-G.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI with blue light significantly increased sensitivity to pinch stimulation of the untreated hindpaw without affecting responses to stimulation of the treated hindpaw.
claims.source: Optogenetic activation of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI with blue light (473 nm, 10 mW) significantly (p<0.0001) increased sensitivity to pinch stimulation of the untreated hindpaw without affecting responses to stimulation of the treated hindpaw or responses in PKCδ-cre mice injected with the control-mCherry virus (Figure 7H).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7H.

claims.claim: Behavioral responses to blue light stimulation are intensity-dependent.
claims.source: Light intensity-response experiments showed that behavioral responses to blue light stimulation are intensity-dependent. Thus, light-induced increases in the sensitivity to pinch of the untreated paw was observed at intensities equal to or higher than 0.6 mW, with a plateau observed starting at 0.8 mW (Figure 7I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7I.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI with blue light at 0.8 mW or 10 mW significantly increased sensitivity to tactile, cold, and heat stimulation of the untreated hindpaw.
claims.source: Consistent with pinch stimulation results, optogenetic activation of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI with blue light at 0.8 mW or 10 mW significantly (P<0.01) increased sensitivity to tactile (Figure 8B), cold (Figure 8C), and heat (Figure 8D) stimulation of the untreated hindpaw.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 8B-D.

claims.claim: Activation of the CeA-PKCδ to ZI inhibitory pathway induces hypersensitivity to tactile, pressure, heat, and cold stimuli in the absence of injury.
claims.source: These results show that activation of the CeA-PKCδ to ZI inhibitory pathway induces hypersensitivity to tactile, pressure, heat, and cold stimuli in the absence of injury.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on optogenetic behavioral data.

claims.claim: Spontaneous ﬁring rates and somatosensory-evoked neuronal responses decrease in the ZI in a rodent model of central pain syndrome.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that spontaneous ﬁring rates and somatosensory-evoked neuronal responses decrease in the ZI in a rodent model of central pain syndrome (Masri et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: The present study showed that the ZI receives moderate axonal terminals from CeA-PKCδ neurons.
claims.source: In the present study, we showed that the ZI receives moderate axonal terminals from CeA-PKCδ neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and that inhibitory inputs from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI contribute to persistent pain-related behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Inhibitory inputs from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI contribute to persistent pain-related behaviors.
claims.source: In the present study, we showed that the ZI receives moderate axonal terminals from CeA-PKCδ neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and that inhibitory inputs from CeA-PKCδ neurons to the ZI contribute to persistent pain-related behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claims.claim: CeA-PKCδ neurons serve as an inhibitory input to the ZI that contributes to the regulation of nociceptive behaviors.
claims.source: It is thus reasonable to postulate that CeA-PKCδ neurons serve as an inhibitory input to the ZI that contributes to the regulation of nociceptive behaviors and provides a mechanistic explanation for the previously reported reductions in ZI activity during pain-related states (Masri et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in the ZI reduced hypersensitivity to pinch, tactile, cold and heat stimulation.
claims.source: At the behavioral level, we showed that optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in the ZI reduced hypersensitivity to pinch, tactile, cold and heat stimulation (Figures 5–6).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figures 5-6.

claims.claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ neurons decreases hypersensitivity to all modalities.
claims.source: These results are consistent with previous studies showing that chemogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ neurons also decreases hypersensitivity to all modalities (Wilson et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Thermal modalities are unaffected by chemogenetic manipulations of ZI-VGAT neurons.
claims.source: Notably, however, our experiments also showed that thermal modalities are unaffected by chemogenetic manipulations of ZI-VGAT neurons (Figures 3–4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figures 3-4.

claims.claim: CeA-PKCδ neurons target a specific subpopulation of ZI neurons that contributes to modulation of all pain modalities.
claims.source: These combined results suggest heterogenous functions of ZI neurons in the modulation of pain-related behaviors, with CeA-PKCδ neurons targeting a specific subpopulation of ZI neurons that contributes to modulation of all pain modalities.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion based on the combined findings.

claims.claim: ZI is a heterogenous structure that contains multiple cell types.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, previous studies have shown that ZI is a heterogenous structure that contains multiple cell types (Mitrofanis, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Heterogeneity of function in the CeA has been previously reported.
claims.source: Heterogeneity of function in the CeA has also been previously reported (Kim et al., 2017; Kong and Zweifel, 2021; Moscarello and Penzo, 2022; Venniro et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claims.claim: CeA-PKCδ and somatostatin-positive CeA neurons have opposing functions in the modulation of pain-related responses.
claims.source: In the context of pain, CeA-PKCδ and somatostatin-positive CeA neurons have been shown to have opposing functions in the modulation of pain-related responses (Wilson et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: CeA-PKCδ neurons provide inhibitory input to the ventral sector of ZI.
claims.source: Our results indicate that CeA-PKCδ neurons provide inhibitory input to the ventral sector of ZI, and that activation of this inhibitory pathway drives behavioral hypersensitivity.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claims.claim: Chemogenetic manipulation of the activity of VGAT-positive ZI neurons bidirectionally modulates pain-related behaviors in a modality-specific manner.
claims.source: In the present study, we show that chemogenetic manipulation of the activity of VGAT-positive ZI neurons bidirectionally modulates pain-related behaviors in a modality-specific manner (Figures 3–4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figures 3-4.

claims.claim: Bilateral hypersensitivity to tactile (but not thermal) stimulation follows inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons in the absence of nerve or tissue injury.
claims.source: Thus, we observe bilateral hypersensitivity to tactile (but not thermal) stimulation following inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons in the absence of nerve or tissue injury (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D.

claims.claim: Chemogenetic activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons reversed nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity to pinch (but not thermal) stimulation.
claims.source: In contrast, chemogenetic activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons reversed nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity to pinch (but not thermal) stimulation (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-D.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation or inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons influences sensitivity to tactile stimulation.
claims.source: Our results are consistent with previous studies that have shown that optogenetic activation or inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons influences sensitivity to tactile stimulation (Hu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Baseline responses in sham animals or the hindpaw contralateral to sciatic nerve treatment were unaltered by chemogenetic activation of ZI-VGAT neurons in the present study.
claims.source: It is important to note that baseline responses in sham animals or the hindpaw contralateral to sciatic nerve treatment were unaltered by chemogenetic activation of ZI-VGAT neurons in the present study.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of ZI-VGAT neurons decreased baseline responses to tactile stimulation in previous studies.
claims.source: This contrasts with previous reports, where optogenetic activation of ZI-VGAT neurons decreased baseline responses to tactile stimulation (Hu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Modulation of behavioral output by optogenetic stimulation is dependent on the frequency and pattern of the stimulation used for the experiments.
claims.source: Previous studies have demonstrated that modulation of behavioral output by optogenetic stimulation is dependent on the frequency and pattern of the stimulation used for the experiments (Padilla-Coreano et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Deep brain stimulation of zona incerta in human subjects reduced experimental heat pain without affecting mechanical pain thresholds.
claims.source: A recent study further demonstrated that deep brain stimulation of zona incerta in human subjects reduced experimental heat pain without affecting mechanical pain thresholds (Lu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Both VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons respond to optogenetic stimulation of CeA terminals in the ZI.
claims.source: In the present study, we evaluated the functional contribution of ZI-VGAT neurons to the modulation of pain-related behaviors. Our optogenetic-assisted circuit mapping experiments showed, however, that both VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons respond to optogenetic stimulation of CeA terminals in the ZI (Figure 2C–D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 2C-D.

claims.claim: Somatostatin-positive CeA neurons project to and inhibit parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons.
claims.source: Consistent with these findings, previous studies have shown that CeA neurons, including somatostatin-positive cells, project to and inhibit parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons (Zhou et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Parvalbumin-positive neurons in the ZI show an opposite electrophysiological phenotype and function in the modulation of pain-related behaviors than ZI-VGAT neurons.
claims.source: Interestingly, this study demonstrated that parvalbumin-positive neurons in the ZI show an opposite electrophysiological phenotype and function in the modulation of pain-related behaviors than what we and others observe for the ZI-VGAT neurons.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion referencing a previous study.

claims.claim: Inhibition of ZI-VGAT neurons drives behavioral hypersensitivity.
claims.source: Thus, while the present and previous studies show that inhibition of ZI-VGAT neurons drives behavioral hypersensitivity, ablation or silencing of parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons was shown to be analgesic (Wang et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Ablation or silencing of parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons was shown to be analgesic.
claims.source: Thus, while the present and previous studies show that inhibition of ZI-VGAT neurons drives behavioral hypersensitivity, ablation or silencing of parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons was shown to be analgesic (Wang et al., 2020).

results.result: CeA-PKCδ neurons project to the zona incerta (ZI) with moderate terminal density restricted to the middle and ventral sectors. Anatomical tracing using AAV-DIO-mCherry and ChrimsonR-tdTomato in PKCδ-cre mice identified 18 brain regions receiving CeA-PKCδ projections, including the ZI. Retrograde tracing confirmed that approximately 19% of ZI-projecting CeA neurons are PKCδ-positive, localized to the capsular and lateral CeA subdivisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C31-C45 provide converging anatomical evidence from multiple approaches (anterograde AAV tracing with two different constructs, retrograde CTB tracing, immunohistochemistry) demonstrating CeA-PKCδ projections to the ZI. The consistency across methods, quantification of transduction efficiency, and anatomical specificity support this result. The semi-quantitative analysis and rostral-caudal mapping provide additional validation.

results.result: The projection from CeA to ZI is monosynaptic and inhibitory. Optogenetic stimulation of ChR2-expressing CeA terminals evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents in 60% of VGAT-positive and 53% of VGAT-negative ZI neurons. These responses persisted in TTX/4-AP, were blocked by bicuculline, and reversed near the chloride equilibrium potential, confirming GABAergic transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C52 provide strong electrophysiological evidence for monosynaptic inhibitory connectivity. The use of TTX/4-AP to confirm monosynaptic transmission, bicuculline to confirm GABAergic signaling, and voltage-clamp recordings at different holding potentials to demonstrate chloride-mediated currents are appropriate controls. The paired-pulse ratio analysis further validates the synaptic nature of the connection.

results.result: Chemogenetic inhibition of VGAT-positive ZI neurons induces bilateral tactile and pressure hypersensitivity in uninjured mice and contralateral hypersensitivity in nerve-injured mice, but does not affect thermal sensitivity. CNO application to hM4Di-transduced ZI neurons significantly reduced firing in slice recordings and produced robust behavioral hypersensitivity that was transient and modality-specific.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C53-C63 demonstrate causal necessity of ZI-VGAT neurons for maintaining normal sensory thresholds. The validation of hM4Di function in slice recordings (C53), histological verification of injection sites (C54-C55), appropriate controls (saline injections, mCherry controls), and statistical significance (p<0.0001) support the behavioral findings. The modality-specificity (tactile/pressure but not thermal) is consistently demonstrated across multiple behavioral assays.

results.result: Chemogenetic activation of VGAT-positive ZI neurons reverses nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity in a modality-specific manner. CNO-mediated activation of hM3Dq-transduced ZI neurons, validated by c-Fos expression, significantly reversed cuff-induced hypersensitivity to pressure stimulation but not thermal stimulation, with effects specific to the injured paw.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C64-C69 demonstrate causal sufficiency of ZI-VGAT neuron activation for reversing injury-induced hypersensitivity. The c-Fos validation of neuronal activation (C64-C65), appropriate controls (saline, mCherry), statistical significance (p<0.0001), and specificity to injured paw (C67) support the conclusion. The modality-specificity (pressure but not thermal) is consistent with the inhibition experiments.

results.result: Optogenetic inhibition of CeA-PKCδ terminals in the ZI reduces nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity across all modalities tested. Yellow light stimulation of NpHR-expressing terminals significantly reduced cuff-induced hypersensitivity to pressure, tactile, cold, and heat stimulation in an intensity-dependent manner, demonstrating that injury-induced activation of this pathway is necessary for maintaining hypersensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C70-C74 provide strong evidence for the necessity of the CeA-PKCδ→ZI pathway in injury-induced hypersensitivity. The validation of NpHR function in slice recordings (C70), intensity-response relationship (C72), effects across multiple sensory modalities (C73), appropriate controls (mCherry), and statistical significance (p<0.0001) support the conclusion. The terminal-specific manipulation is more precise than somatic manipulations.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of CeA-PKCδ terminals in the ZI induces hypersensitivity in uninjured paws across all sensory modalities. Blue light stimulation of ChR2-expressing terminals significantly increased sensitivity to pressure, tactile, cold, and heat stimulation in the uninjured paw in an intensity-dependent manner, demonstrating that activation of this pathway is sufficient to induce hypersensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C76-C80 demonstrate causal sufficiency of the CeA-PKCδ→ZI pathway for inducing hypersensitivity. The validation of ChR2 function in slice recordings (C76), intensity-response relationship (C78), effects across all sensory modalities (C79), appropriate controls (mCherry), and statistical significance (p<0.0001 or p<0.01) support the conclusion. The specificity to the uninjured paw (C77) is notable.

results.result: The CeA-PKCδ to ZI pathway is an inhibitory efferent pathway that bidirectionally modulates pain-related behaviors. The authors conclude that CeA-PKCδ neurons provide inhibitory input to the ventral ZI, and that this pathway contributes to the regulation of nociceptive behaviors and provides a mechanistic explanation for previously reported reductions in ZI activity during pain states.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C82-C84, C92 represent the main conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the convergence of anatomical (C3, C31-C45), electrophysiological (C46-C52), and behavioral evidence (C5-C9, C53-C80). The bidirectional modulation is demonstrated by both loss-of-function (inhibition reduces hypersensitivity) and gain-of-function (activation induces hypersensitivity) experiments with appropriate controls.

results.result: Chemogenetic manipulation of ZI-VGAT neurons shows modality-specific effects, with thermal modalities unaffected while tactile/pressure modalities are bidirectionally modulated. The authors suggest this indicates that CeA-PKCδ neurons target a specific subpopulation of ZI neurons that contributes to modulation of all pain modalities.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88, C93-C95 highlight a discrepancy between chemogenetic manipulation of ZI-VGAT neurons (modality-specific effects) and optogenetic manipulation of CeA-PKCδ terminals in ZI (all modalities affected). While C88 is an interpretation that attempts to reconcile this, it remains speculative without direct evidence identifying the specific ZI subpopulation targeted by CeA-PKCδ neurons. Additional experiments (e.g., cell-type-specific recordings, molecular profiling) would be needed to support this interpretation.

results.result: Both VGAT-positive and VGAT-negative ZI neurons respond to CeA terminal stimulation, and the authors propose a model where injury-induced inhibition of somatostatin-expressing CeA neurons disinhibits parvalbumin-positive ZI neurons while injury-induced activation of CeA-PKCδ neurons inhibits VGAT-positive ZI neurons, both resulting in behavioral hypersensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C111 present an integrative model based on the current findings and prior literature. While C101 is supported by the electrophysiology data (C48-C49), and C102-C109 accurately cite prior work, the predictions in C110-C111 are speculative and not directly tested in this study. The model is plausible but requires additional experiments to validate the proposed parallel pathways and their interactions.
